PindariCoders started as a university dream: a little place to build things and help others learn coding.

That idea sat on the shelf for a while. This is it finding its way back—one small experiment, one useful note, one finished thing at a time.

You don’t have to know everything to make something. There’s room here to figure it out.

FIELD NOTE 01 / CSS

Which way is the main axis, anyway?

Flexbox gets easier when you stop thinking of justify-content as “horizontal alignment.” It follows the main axis, and you get to choose that axis.

With flex-direction: row, items follow the inline direction—usually left to right in English. With column, they follow the block direction—usually top to bottom.

Two properties, two jobs

justify-content distributes available space along the main axis. align-items aligns items along the cross axis. Change the direction and their visual roles change with it.

Try it in the lab

Choose space-between in “a little flex.” The outer boxes move to the edges; available space goes between them. Choose center and the group sits in the middle, keeping the gap you set.

If nothing moves, check whether the container has any extra space to distribute. Alignment can’t create spare room.

Go deeper on MDN ↗

FIELD NOTE 02 / DESIGN

Your font size is only half the story.

A heading can be huge and still feel awkward. The space inside and around the words does just as much work as the size.

Start with the words

Use your actual headline when choosing a typeface. A beautiful “Aa” sample doesn’t tell you how a long sentence will wrap on a phone.

Give each size its own rhythm

Large headings can often use tighter letter spacing. Small text usually needs more breathing room. Treat both as starting points to inspect, not rules to apply blindly.

Line height controls the distance between lines. Try roughly 1.5 for paragraphs, then check the actual font. Headings can be tighter, but tall letters and descenders must never collide.

One small experiment

Open “type something.” Keep the words the same and change only the typeface. Next, change the letter spacing. Look for the point where a little character becomes hard to read.

Then test your page on a narrow screen and with enlarged text. Good typography still works when the reader changes the conditions.

FIELD NOTE 03 / BUILDING

A small finished thing is a good place to start.

You can make a useful project before you feel ready to build a platform. Pick one person, one problem, and one thing the page should let them do.

Make the finish line visible

“Build a developer toolkit” has no obvious end. “Let someone pick two colors and check their contrast” has a clear result you can test.

Write that result down before opening your editor. When the project begins growing extra features, come back to it.

Let someone use it

Share a working link with a friend. Give them a task, then watch without explaining the interface. Where they hesitate is useful feedback.

Keep the lesson

Write down one thing that broke and how you fixed it. That’s already the beginning of a helpful post. It doesn’t need to be a complete course.

Finishing something small gives you something real to improve—and a much better starting point for the next idea.
